faqs.q: How long should you spend in Piazza del Campo?

articles.bodyHtml:
Piazza del Campo is the best free thing in Tuscany, and the one most travellers get slightly wrong. They photograph it from the upper curve, sit for twenty minutes, pay eight euro for a coffee at a terrace table, and leave without seeing what the square is actually saying.

It is also, as of 2026, a square with rules — including one that turns the classic Siena picnic into a fineable act. Start there, because it is the part nobody tells you.

Quick answer

You can sit on the Campo. You cannot lie down on it, and you cannot eat on it. A Comune ordinance, extended to 30 September 2026, prohibits sleeping, lying down and placing bedding in public squares, and prohibits consuming food on the steps of public buildings and in Piazza del Campo in front of the Palazzo Pubblico. Sanctions across the ordinance run from €50 to €480.

Sitting on the brick is not itself banned — the point was debated publicly when the ordinance was made, and ordinary sitting was not prohibited. The sandwich is the problem, not the sitting.

Allow 45 minutes for the square alone, and walk the full perimeter rather than standing at one viewpoint. Early morning for the space, the hour before sunset for the light and the life. It costs nothing, it never closes, and it is the one sight in Siena you cannot exhaust.

The 2026 rules, plainly

Siena tightened its urban-decorum regime across 2025–26, and a traveller who last visited a few years ago will find the Campo governed differently.

What the ordinance prohibits, as published: sleeping, lying down, and placing mattresses, bedding or camping objects in squares, green areas, porticoes and around monuments; and consuming food on the steps of public buildings, and in Piazza del Campo in front of the Palazzo Pubblico. Enforcement measures include immediate removal, clearing of occupied areas, and in serious cases referral for prosecution. Administrative fines run from €50 to €480.

What it does not prohibit: sitting. The ordinance drew local political criticism precisely on this point — one opposition line was that "Piazza del Campo is not a drawing room" — and ordinary sitting on the square was not made an offence. The separate historic-centre regulation does prohibit sitting on church steps, which is a different rule in a different place and worth remembering as you walk around the cathedral.

How to read this as a visitor. The ordinance's wording ties the food ban to the area in front of the Palazzo Pubblico, and we could not establish whether it is enforced across the whole shell or only that section. Treat the entire Campo as somewhere you do not eat. Buy the schiacciata, walk two minutes to the Orto de' Pecci or up to the Fortezza, and eat there instead. The saving on a terrace lunch is real; a €480 exposure to save it is not a trade worth making.

One apparent exception we cannot resolve for you. The Comune authorises events that put food on the square — most visibly the Mercato nel Campo, the December market whose stalls sell and serve on the shell. The ordinance is aimed at people consuming their own food there; how it interacts with licensed event catering is not something we could establish from the published wording. If you are here for an authorised market, do what the market is set up for; the rest of the year, assume your own sandwich is not welcome.

And the date matters. This ordinance has been extended repeatedly rather than made permanent, and the current extension runs to 30 September 2026. If you are travelling after that, check whether it was renewed again — the direction of travel in Siena, as in Florence, is toward more regulation of the historic centre rather than less.

Reading the square: what you are standing on

Most guides call the Campo shell-shaped and stop. The shape is an argument, and it is legible from the ground once you know what to look for.

The paving was laid between 1327 and 1349, in knife-shaped red brick, and it is divided by ten lines of white travertine into nine segments that all converge on the Palazzo Pubblico at the low point.

The nine are the Governo dei Nove — the merchant oligarchy that governed Siena from the 1280s to the 1350s, the most stable stretch in the city's history and the regime that commissioned nearly everything visitors come to see. Nine segments, nine governors, all pointing at the building they governed from. The same nine folds are also read as the folds of the Virgin's cloak; Siena declared the Virgin its sovereign, not merely its patron, and the square is a floor laid under her.

The slope is not a defect. The Campo occupies the junction of the three ridges Siena is built on — the meeting point of the city's three terzi — and was a market field before it was a piazza, which is where the name comes from. Its inward tilt means everyone standing in it faces the seat of government and everyone can see everyone else. That was the point. It is also why the Palio works: the crowd fills the dish, the horses run the rim.

Do this, and the square opens up: stand at the top of the curve for the full view, then walk down the slope to the Palazzo Pubblico and turn round. From below, the enclosing palazzi form a continuous, unbroken wall of façades — the result of a fourteenth-century building code that regulated window forms around the square. Very few medieval squares in Europe held that discipline for seven hundred years.

The Fonte Gaia is a copy, and the originals are worth finding

The fountain on the upper curve is the Fonte Gaia, and what you are photographing is a nineteenth-century replacement.

Jacopo della Quercia carved the original in the 1410s, finishing in 1419 — a Madonna and Child flanked by the Virtues, with Justice among them, deliberately echoing the imagery of Lorenzetti's Good Government frescoes inside the Palazzo Pubblico a few metres away. The square and the town hall were making the same argument in stone and paint.

By the nineteenth century the marble had deteriorated badly, and in 1858 the ensemble was replaced in situ by a free adaptation carved by Tito Sarrocchi. That is what stands there now. The surviving original fragments are displayed in Santa Maria della Scala, the former hospital facing the cathedral — which is a good reason to buy the €20 combined ticket described below, and one that almost no visitor knows.

The Palazzo Pubblico and the Museo Civico

The Palazzo Pubblico closes the low side of the square and still houses Siena's city government. The Museo Civico occupies its historic rooms, and it holds the single most important thing on the Campo: Ambrogio Lorenzetti's Allegory and Effects of Good and Bad Government, painted 1338–1339 in the Sala dei Nove — the room where the nine governors actually met, with a picture of the consequences of their own decisions wrapped around them. It is the most significant secular painting cycle to survive from medieval Europe, and it is in the room it was painted for.

The 2026 prices and hours, checked 16 August 2026:

TicketPriceNotes
Museo Civico€10.00€11.00 with booking
Museo Civico + Torre del Mangia€15.00Valid 1 day; not bookable
Museo Civico + Santa Maria della Scala€14.00Valid 2 days; €15.00 with booking
Museo Civico + Santa Maria della Scala + Torre€20.00Not bookable
  • Summer, 1 March to 31 October: 10:00–13:45 and 14:30–19:00, ticket office closing 18:15.
  • Winter, 1 November to 28 February: 10:00–13:00 and 13:45–16:00, ticket office closing 15:15.

Read the ticket-office time rather than the closing time, and note that the winter counter shuts at 15:15 — a winter visitor who lunches slowly has lost the museum, not just the queue.

The chapel most people walk straight past

At the foot of the Torre, leaning against the Palazzo Pubblico, is an open marble loggia that thousands of visitors photograph by accident and almost nobody looks at. It is the Cappella di Piazza, and it is the most direct surviving statement of what 1348 did to this city.

Siena built it in fulfilment of a vow made during the plague — an open-air chapel on the civic square, promised by a population that had just lost a catastrophic share of itself. The pillars went up between 1352 and 1376 under Domenico di Agostino and then Giovanni di Cecco; the corner pilasters took their present form in 1378, with sculpture carved in 1378–1382 by Mariano d'Angelo Romanelli and Bartolomeo di Tommé. A century later, between 1463 and 1468, Antonio Federighi added the Renaissance arches and the covering that give it its present monumental look — which is why the chapel reads as two centuries stacked on each other, because it is.

The fresco that once stood above its altar, a Madonna and Child with God the Father painted by Il Sodoma between 1537 and 1539, no longer weathers on the square; what survives of it is inside the Museo Civico. Worth knowing before you buy the ticket: the chapel outside and the fragment inside are the same object, separated.

Stand in front of it for one minute. The tower behind it was finished in 1348 and the chapel in front of it was promised in the same year, for opposite reasons — civic confidence and civic terror, built four metres apart.

The Torre del Mangia, briefly

The tower beside the Palazzo Pubblico is the climb that gives you the Campo from directly above, and it comes with rules that decide the day: it cannot be pre-booked at all, ascents run every 45 minutes for 25 people, and on a combined ticket your first entry must be at the tower rather than the museum.

Those constraints are why the €15 combination is worth buying at the ticket office first thing rather than mid-afternoon. Our Torre del Mangia guide sets out the full price ladder, the ascent times, the official health warnings and the case for the Facciatone instead.

When to be on the Campo

The square changes character more than any other space in Siena, and the difference between a good visit and a memorable one is an hour of timing.

  • Before 09:00. The Campo belongs to Siena — deliveries, dog walkers, people crossing to work. The best photographs and the only time the space feels large.
  • 10:00 to 16:00. Peak. Day-trip coaches from Florence unload into these hours, the terraces fill, and the square is at its least atmospheric and most expensive.
  • The hour before sunset. The brick warms to a colour that has no equivalent, the slope fills with people sitting, and the Torre throws a shadow across the shell. If you only stand here once, stand here then.
  • After dark. The Palazzo Pubblico is lit and the square empties slowly. Quietly one of the best things about staying overnight rather than day-tripping — a distinction our day trip versus overnight comparison is built around.

Seasonally: the Campo is at its best in late spring and from mid-September through October. In high summer the unshaded brick radiates heat well into the evening, and in deep winter the wind funnels down the ridges into it.

Eating and drinking around the Campo

Two honest facts, given that eating on the square is now restricted.

The terraces charge for the view, and that is a legitimate transaction. A coffee or an aperitivo at a Campo table costs a multiple of the same drink two streets away, and you are buying an hour in one of Europe's great rooms. Do it once, deliberately, at the hour you most want to be there — and read the price list before sitting, because table service and terrace surcharges are normal and legal here.

For actual meals, walk away from the shell. The rule that holds across Siena holds hardest here: quality rises and prices fall within two streets of the Campo. Our Siena eating guide covers the streets worth walking into.

And for a picnic — now that the square itself is out — the Orto de' Pecci below the walls and the Fortezza Medicea are the two obvious places, both a few minutes' walk, both free, both with a view.

The Campo during the Palio

Twice a year the square stops being a square. A track of tuff is laid around the outside of the shell, stands go up against the palazzi, and the centre becomes standing room for the crowd. The races run on 2 July and 16 August, with four days of trials, drawings and processions before each.

For those periods, everything above is suspended: the surface is different, access is controlled, the Museo Civico and Torre run special published hours, and the ordinary business of sitting on the brick is not available. If your dates fall in late June, early July or mid-August, read our Palio guide before planning anything on the Campo — including the honest case for choosing a different week.

How Piazza del Campo fits a Siena day

The Campo is the hub and should be visited more than once rather than ticked off. A workable shape: cross it early on the way to the Museo Civico ticket office, climb the tower on the first slot, see the Lorenzetti frescoes, walk up to the cathedral complex for the afternoon, and come back to the Campo for the last hour of light.

Our one day in Siena itinerary lays out the walking, and the cathedral ticket guide covers the other half of the day — including the Facciatone, which gives you the view of Siena with the Torre del Mangia in it.

How we checked these details

Checked 16 August 2026, by web research; direct page fetches are blocked in our environment, so this rests on search-surfaced material rather than pages we opened.

Verified against the Comune di Siena and municipal-museum sources: the anti-bivouac ordinance extended to 30 September 2026, its prohibitions on sleeping, lying down and placing bedding in public squares and around monuments, its prohibition on consuming food on the steps of public buildings and in Piazza del Campo in front of the Palazzo Pubblico, the enforcement measures, and the €50–€480 sanction range; the fact that ordinary sitting was not made an offence, and that this was publicly contested at the time; the separate historic-centre rule prohibiting sitting on church steps while permitting paid tables; and the Museo Civico's 2026 prices (€10.00, €11.00 with booking) and combined tickets at €15.00, €14.00/€15.00 and €20.00, together with the summer hours of 10:00–13:45 and 14:30–19:00 with the ticket office closing at 18:15 and the winter hours of 10:00–13:00 and 13:45–16:00 with the office closing at 15:15.

Verified against reference and regional tourism sources: the paving laid between 1327 and 1349 in knife-shaped brick, divided by ten travertine lines into nine segments converging on the Palazzo Pubblico; the reading of those nine as the Governo dei Nove, who governed from the 1280s to the 1350s, and as the folds of the Virgin's cloak; the Fonte Gaia carved by Jacopo della Quercia and finished in 1419, its imagery of the Madonna and Child with the Virtues including Justice, its replacement in situ by Tito Sarrocchi's adaptation in 1858, and the display of the surviving originals in Santa Maria della Scala; Ambrogio Lorenzetti's Allegory and Effects of Good and Bad Government, painted 1338–1339 in the Sala dei Nove; and the Cappella di Piazza — its origin as a vow made during the 1348 plague, the 1352–1376 construction under Domenico di Agostino and Giovanni di Cecco, the 1378 pilasters with sculpture of 1378–1382 by Mariano d'Angelo Romanelli and Bartolomeo di Tommé, Antonio Federighi's 1463–1468 Renaissance remodelling, and Il Sodoma's 1537–1539 altar fresco whose remains are now in the Museo Civico.

Flagged as unconfirmed: how the food prohibition interacts with authorised events that serve on the square, such as the December Mercato nel Campo; whether the prohibition is enforced across the whole Campo or only the section in front of the Palazzo Pubblico — the ordinance's wording admits both readings, and we advise treating the whole square as off-limits; whether the ordinance will be extended beyond 30 September 2026, as it has been repeatedly before; and the exact Palio-period Museo Civico and Torre hours, which the Comune publishes close to each race. Sources differ on whether Jacopo della Quercia began the Fonte Gaia in 1408 or 1414, so we give only the completion date, which they agree on.

We have no commercial relationship with the Comune di Siena, any museum or any bar or restaurant on or near the square. No booking made from this page pays us anything.

Final thoughts

The Campo does not need a ticket, a slot or a plan, which is exactly why people give it twenty minutes and move on. Give it three visits in a day instead — early, mid-afternoon on the way past, and the last hour of light — and it does something no single sight in Siena manages, which is to stop being a monument and start being a place.

Just do not eat your lunch on it. Seven hundred years of civic self-regard have produced, among other things, a fine of up to €480.

articles.excerpt: Siena Cathedral stopped being one ticket in March 2026. There are now three routes at three prices, all of them keyed to whether the marble floor is uncovered — and a free winter window that almost no guide mentions. This guide sets out what each route contains, what it costs in both states of the floor, and which one is worth your money.

faqs.q: How much are Siena Cathedral tickets in 2026?
faqs.a: It depends which of the three routes you buy and whether the marble floor is uncovered. Cathedral plus Piccolomini Library is €5.00, rising to €8.00 with the floor uncovered. The OPA SI Pass, covering the whole complex, is €13.00 and €15.00. The Gate of Heaven roof route is a separate €7.00 and €10.00. All tickets are valid three consecutive days.

faqs.q: Is Siena Cathedral free?
faqs.a: In winter, largely yes. The Opera has published free cathedral entry from 1 November to 24 December and from 7 January to 28 February, with the Piccolomini Library at €2.00 and the OPA SI Pass reduced to €8.00. People born in or resident in Siena enter free year-round. Note that the free-winter window overlaps the uncovered-floor period between 1 and 15 November, and the Opera does not say which rule governs those dates — budget the uncovered-floor fare.

faqs.q: When is the Siena Cathedral floor uncovered in 2026?
faqs.a: From 27 June to 31 July, and again from 18 August to 15 November 2026. It is covered from 1 January to 26 June, from 1 to 17 August, and from 16 November to 31 December. The August gap catches people out: the floor is boarded over during Ferragosto week and the 16 August Palio.

faqs.q: Is the OPA SI Pass worth it?
faqs.a: For anyone with half a day or more, clearly yes. It costs roughly two and a half times the cathedral-only ticket and adds the Museo dell'Opera with Duccio's Maestà, the panorama from the unfinished façade, the Baptistery, the Crypt, the Oratory of San Bernardino and the Sotto il Duomo videomapping route. Buy the cathedral-only ticket instead if you have ninety minutes and a fixed departure.

faqs.q: Is the Gate of Heaven included in the OPA SI Pass?
faqs.a: No. The Gate of Heaven is a separate ticket at €7.00, or €10.00 with the floor uncovered, and it must be booked — online or at the ticket office subject to remaining availability. Numbers are limited by the walkways themselves, and it is the part of the complex where turning up hopeful most often fails.

faqs.q: Where should you buy Siena Cathedral tickets?
faqs.a: Direct from the Opera: online, through its call centre, or at the ticket offices at Piazza Duomo 7 and the Dear Guests visitor centre at Via di Città 48 near Piazza del Campo. The Via di Città office is the useful one — it is on the walk up from the Campo and usually quieter. Third-party sites list the pass well above face value.

faqs.q: What is the dress code for Siena Cathedral?
faqs.a: Shoulders and knees covered, for everyone, and it is enforced at the door. This is an active cathedral, so Sunday mornings, feast days and services also restrict or close visitor access — check the official calendar for your date rather than assuming the published hours apply every day.

articles.bodyHtml:
Siena Cathedral is not a single-room attraction, and since March 2026 it is not a single ticket either. The Opera della Metropolitana reorganised how the complex is visited, and the result is three separate routes at three separate prices — with a fourth situation, free winter entry, that almost no guide mentions.

If you have read an older article quoting one price for everything, that structure no longer exists. This page explains what replaced it, what each route actually contains, and which one is worth your money.

Quick answer

There are three routes, not one pass. The cathedral with the Piccolomini Library is the cheap entry. The OPA SI Pass is the full circuit and includes the underground Sotto il Duomo — Percorsi di Luce videomapping route. The Gate of Heaven is a separate, bookable climb into the roof structure.

Every price moves with one thing: whether the marble floor is uncovered. In 2026 that is 27 June to 31 July and 18 August to 15 November.

For most first-time visitors with half a day, the OPA SI Pass at €13 (€15 with the floor uncovered) is the right buy — it is valid three consecutive days, so it survives a change of plan. If you have ninety minutes and only want the building itself, take the cathedral and library ticket instead.

The 2026 prices, by route

Checked against the Opera's own published tariffs on 16 August 2026. The columns are the two states of the floor.

RouteFloor coveredFloor uncovered
Cathedral + Piccolomini Library€5.00€8.00
OPA SI Pass (full complex + Sotto il Duomo)€13.00€15.00
Gate of Heaven (roof route)€7.00€10.00

Two further rates are published: reduced entry at €8.00 for groups over 14 and groups with a guide during the uncovered-floor period, and free admission for anyone born in or resident in Siena, which covers both the cathedral and the OPA SI Pass route. If you are staying with local hosts, it is worth knowing that the person showing you round may walk in free.

All tickets are valid for three consecutive days from the date of issue. This is the most underused feature of the complex: you are not buying one afternoon, you are buying a window. Split the museum off from the cathedral and do them on different days when the light and your legs suit.

What changed in March 2026, and why older guides are wrong

Until this year the complex was sold largely as one pass. From March 2026 the Opera separated the visit into the three routes above and repriced them, adding the underground videomapping route to the OPA SI Pass and pulling the roof climb out as its own bookable product.

The practical consequence for a traveller is that almost every English-language page describing Siena Cathedral tickets is now describing a product that no longer exists at that price. Figures in circulation from the previous structure — and resale prices well above face value — are still the top results for the obvious searches. Before you pay anything, check the price against the two states of the floor calendar below; if a seller cannot tell you which state your date falls in, they are not looking at the official tariff.

The floor: the single fact that governs everything

Siena's cathedral floor is fifty-six inlaid marble panels worked between the fourteenth and the sixteenth centuries — a narrative pavement that Vasari called the most beautiful, largest and most magnificent ever made. For most of the year it is boarded over to protect it, and you walk across plain covering without seeing any of it.

In 2026 the floor is uncovered from 27 June to 31 July, and again from 18 August to 15 November. Outside those windows — 1 January to 26 June, 1 to 17 August, and 16 November to 31 December — it is covered.

Three things follow that are worth planning around:

  • The two-week August gap is real and catches people out. The floor goes back under cover for the first seventeen days of August, which includes the Palio of 16 August and the Ferragosto week when Siena is at its fullest. Arriving in that fortnight expecting the marble is the most common disappointment at this cathedral.
  • The uncovering runs deep into November. Mid-October to mid-November gives you the floor, thin crowds and low autumn light through the nave at the same time — the best combination the cathedral offers all year, and the reason our November guide rates the month more highly than most.
  • The uncovered price is not a surcharge on a normal visit. You are paying a few euro more to see the thing the building is most famous for. When the floor is up, the cathedral is a different room.

The free winter window, and the ambiguity in it

This is the best-value fact on this page and the one least likely to appear elsewhere. The Opera has published free cathedral entry across the winter months — 1 November to 24 December, and 7 January to 28 February — with the Piccolomini Library at €2.00 and the OPA SI Pass reduced to €8.00.

For a traveller that is a serious saving. A winter visit to Siena that includes the cathedral, the library and the full pass costs less than the cathedral alone in July.

Now the honest caveat, because the two published calendars overlap. The floor is uncovered until 15 November, and the uncovered-floor tariff applies in that period; the free-winter announcement begins on 1 November. The Opera's own pages do not resolve which rule governs 1–15 November, and we could not establish it. Our advice for those dates: budget the uncovered-floor fares — €8 for cathedral and library, €15 for the pass — and treat free entry as an upside rather than a plan. From 16 November the two calendars agree and the winter rates are unambiguous.

Which route to buy

Cathedral + Piccolomini Library — €5, or €8 with the floor

The cheap, focused visit. You get the striped nave, Nicola Pisano's pulpit, the dome, and the library — a small frescoed room off the north aisle where Pinturicchio and his workshop painted ten scenes from the life of Pius II between 1503 and 1508, in colours that look as though they were finished last year. Ninety minutes is enough.

Buy this if: you are on a day trip with a fixed return bus, you have already committed the afternoon elsewhere, or the museum circuit does not appeal.

OPA SI Pass — €13, or €15 with the floor

The full complex: the cathedral and library, the Museo dell'Opera (Duccio's Maestà, the altarpiece carried through the streets in 1311, is here and is the single greatest object in Siena), the panorama from the unfinished façade, the Baptistery, the Crypt, the Oratory of San Bernardino, and the Sotto il Duomo — Percorsi di Luce route.

Buy this if: you have half a day or more, or any interest in painting. The arithmetic is not close — the pass costs roughly two and a half times the cathedral ticket and contains six or seven times as much.

Gate of Heaven — €7, or €10 with the floor

A guided route up into the structure above the nave, along walkways inside the roof, with views down into the cathedral and out over the city from a height nothing else in Siena offers. It is a separate ticket, it is not included in the OPA SI Pass, and it must be booked — online or at the ticket office subject to remaining availability. Numbers are limited by the walkways themselves.

Buy this if: you have booked ahead and you are comfortable on narrow stairs at height. It is the one part of the complex that genuinely sells out, and the one where turning up hopeful fails most often.

Sotto il Duomo — Percorsi di Luce

The underground route now bundled into the OPA SI Pass deserves its own paragraph, because the name tells you nothing.

It runs from the Baptistery down through the spaces created by the cathedral's enlargement begun in 1317 — under the foundations of the left transept — and ends in the seventeenth-century hall of the Oratory of San Giovannino, a church that had been closed to the public for decades before the route recovered it. The journey is staged as a 3D videomapping projection using around forty laser projectors, with multilingual headsets.

It divides opinion, and honestly: if you came to Siena for medieval painting, this is not that, and you may find the son-et-lumière treatment at odds with the building. If you are travelling with teenagers, or with anyone whose patience for altarpieces is finite, it is the part of the complex they will talk about afterwards. Either way you are no longer choosing — it is inside the pass.

Opening hours in 2026

As published for the periods concerned, checked 16 August 2026:

  • During the uncovered-floor periods (27 June–31 July, 18 August–30 October): 10:00–19:00, with public holidays 09:30–18:00.
  • 1 November to 24 December: 10:30–17:30.
  • Last admission is 30 minutes before closing across the complex.

Two cautions. The cathedral is a working church: Sunday mornings, feast days and services restrict or close visitor access, and the schedule is not the same for every component of the complex. And individual sites within the complex keep their own hours, so a plan that assumes the museum is open because the cathedral is will occasionally fail. Check the official calendar for your specific date — the hours above are the pattern, not a promise for every day.

Where to buy, and how to avoid paying twice

Tickets are sold online, through the Opera's call centre, and at two physical offices: Piazza Duomo 7, beside the cathedral, and the "Dear Guests" visitor centre at Via di Città 48, near Piazza del Campo. The second is the useful one — it is on the walk up from the Campo, it is usually quieter than the cathedral window, and buying there means you arrive at the Duomo holding a ticket rather than joining a queue in the sun.

Resale markups are the main risk here. Third-party sites list the OPA SI Pass well above the Opera's own price, and some bundle it with services you have not asked for. The Opera sells directly. If a price does not match the table above for your date's floor state, you are looking at a markup, an old tariff, or both.

Guided visits of the museum complex with authorised guides are arranged at the ticket office rather than online.

Dress code, accessibility and how long to allow

Dress code. This is an active cathedral and the rule is enforced at the door: shoulders and knees covered, for everyone. In July a thin scarf in the day bag is the difference between walking in and walking back to the hotel.

Accessibility. The cathedral and museum are broadly manageable; the Gate of Heaven is not — it is stairs and narrow walkways by definition, and the panorama from the unfinished façade is reached by a climb. Anyone with mobility limitations should plan the pass around the ground-level components and treat the high routes as optional.

Time. Cathedral and library, ninety minutes. Add the Museo dell'Opera and the façade panorama and you are at three hours. The whole complex including the underground route and the Gate of Heaven is a full day, which is precisely why the three-day validity matters — split it. Our one day in Siena itinerary shows how the cathedral fits a single-day visit, and the day trip versus overnight comparison covers whether one day is enough at all.

How we checked these details

Checked 16 August 2026, by web research against the Opera della Metropolitana's own published material; direct page fetches are blocked in our environment, so this rests on search-surfaced official content rather than pages we opened.

Verified: the March 2026 reorganisation into three visit routes; the cathedral and Piccolomini Library at €5.00 rising to €8.00 with the floor uncovered; the OPA SI Pass at €13.00 and €15.00; the Gate of Heaven at €7.00 and €10.00 across the same two states; the €8.00 reduced rate for groups over 14 and guided groups during the uncovered period; free access for those born in or resident in Siena, covering the cathedral and the OPA SI Pass; three-consecutive-day validity; the 2026 floor-uncovering periods of 27 June–31 July and 18 August–15 November, with the covered bands of 1 January–26 June, 1–17 August and 16 November–31 December; the free winter cathedral entry of 1 November–24 December and 7 January–28 February with the library at €2.00 and the pass at €8.00; the components of the complex including the Museo dell'Opera, the unfinished-façade panorama, the Baptistery, the Crypt and the Oratory of San Bernardino; the Sotto il Duomo — Percorsi di Luce route from the Baptistery to the Oratory of San Giovannino through the spaces of the 1317 enlargement, presented by 3D videomapping with around forty laser projectors and multilingual headsets; the Pinturicchio workshop frescoes of 1503–1508 in the Piccolomini Library; the ticket offices at Piazza Duomo 7 and Via di Città 48; the requirement to book the Gate of Heaven; and the published opening hours of 10:00–19:00 in the uncovered period with 09:30–18:00 on public holidays, 10:30–17:30 from 1 November to 24 December, and last admission 30 minutes before closing.

Conflicts we could not resolve, stated rather than smoothed over. First, the free-winter window and the uncovered-floor period overlap between 1 and 15 November 2026, and the Opera's pages do not say which governs; we tell you to budget the uncovered-floor fare for those dates. Second, an older tariff of €14 and €16 for the OPA SI Pass remains findable on the Opera's own site alongside the new €13 and €15; we have followed the March 2026 reorganisation announcement, which is the more recent and more specific source, but you should expect to see both figures while you research. Third, one official page gives the uncovered period's summer hours as running to 30 October while the tariff calendar runs the uncovered period to 15 November — so the hours for the first fortnight of November are the ones most worth confirming for your date.

Also unconfirmed: the current reduced and child rates for each of the three routes under the new structure, the 2027 floor calendar and tariffs, and Gate of Heaven session times and group sizes. Prices and calendars at this complex changed materially in 2026 — verify on the Opera's own channels before relying on any figure here.

We have no commercial relationship with the Opera della Metropolitana or any ticket seller. No booking made from this page pays us anything, and no reseller is recommended.

Final thoughts

The cathedral is the reason a great many people come to Siena, and it is the one attraction here where the ticket decision genuinely changes the visit rather than just the bill. Get the floor state right, buy the pass rather than the cheap entry unless your day is genuinely short, and use the three days you have paid for instead of compressing everything into one exhausted afternoon.

And if your dates are flexible at all: come between mid-October and mid-November. The marble is up, the queues are gone, and the cathedral does the thing it was built to do — turn ordinary daylight into something worth having travelled for.

articles.excerpt: The Torre del Mangia cannot be booked online, admits 25 people every 45 minutes, closes its ticket counter before the museum shuts, and — on a combined ticket — insists you climb before you visit anything else. articles.bodyHtml:
The Torre del Mangia is the climb everyone photographs from below and a surprising number never make. Not because it is sold out in the way Florence's museums are, but because of two rules that almost no guide states plainly — and that quietly wreck a lot of Siena afternoons.

Quick answer

You cannot pre-book it. Tickets that include the tower are not bookable online and are sold only at the Museo Civico and Torre del Mangia ticket office in the Palazzo Pubblico. Every "skip the line Torre del Mangia" offer you find elsewhere is selling you something else.

Ascents run every 45 minutes for a maximum of 25 people. That is roughly 25 people per slot, twelve slots a day in summer. On a busy afternoon the next available slot can be hours away, and it is allocated at the counter, not by an algorithm.

And the rule that ruins itineraries: if you buy a combined ticket, your first entry must be at the tower. Museum first, tower second is not permitted. Plan the day around the tower slot and fit the Museo Civico around it.

The move: go to the ticket office early — before 10:00 if you can — buy the €15 Museo Civico + Torre combination, take the earliest slot offered, and see the Lorenzetti frescoes afterwards. If the slots are gone or the weather is wrong, the Facciatone is a genuine substitute and is covered below.

The 2026 prices

Published by the Comune di Siena and checked on 16 August 2026. Note that the booking surcharge exists only on tickets that do not include the tower — because tower tickets cannot be booked at all.

TicketPriceNotes
Torre del Mangia only€10.00Ticket office only
Torre del Mangia, family€25.002 adults + minors aged 11–18
Museo Civico only€10.00€11.00 with booking
Museo Civico + Torre del Mangia€15.00Valid 1 day; not bookable
Museo Civico + Santa Maria della Scala€14.00Valid 2 days; €15.00 with booking
Museo Civico + Santa Maria della Scala + Torre€20.00Not bookable

The €15 combination is the obvious buy. The tower alone is €10 and the museum alone is €10; together they are €15, so the museum effectively costs five euro. The Museo Civico holds Ambrogio Lorenzetti's Allegory and Effects of Good and Bad Government — the most important secular painting cycle to survive from medieval Europe, painted in the room where the men it was lecturing actually sat. Five euro is not a price for that. It is a rounding error.

The €20 triple adds Santa Maria della Scala across the piazza from the cathedral — the vast former hospital that is the most underrated building in Siena. If you have a full day, take it.

The three rules that catch people out

1. No booking, ticket office only

Tickets including the tower are not reservable and are sold exclusively at the Museo Civico and Torre del Mangia ticket office. There is no official online slot release, no timed-entry email, no app.

The practical consequence: your position in the day is decided by when you physically arrive at the counter. This is unusual enough in 2026 that visitors assume they have simply failed to find the booking page. They have not. It does not exist.

2. On a combined ticket, the tower comes first

The Comune's own condition is explicit: where a combined ticket is purchased, the first entry must be made at the Torre del Mangia. You cannot spend two hours in the Museo Civico and then climb.

This inverts the instinctive order — most people want to do the indoor thing first and save the view for late light — and it is the single most common reason a Siena afternoon collapses. Build the day the other way round.

3. Twenty-five people, every forty-five minutes

Ascents are released in slots of 45 minutes with a cap of 25 people. In the summer season the published ascent times are 10:00, 10:45, 11:30, 12:15, 13:00, 13:45, 14:30, 15:15, 16:00, 16:45, 17:30 and 18:00.

Twelve slots at twenty-five people is a ceiling of about three hundred climbers a day. Siena receives many multiples of that in high season. The arithmetic is the whole story: this is a scarce ticket that behaves like an unscarce one, because nothing warns you until you are at the counter.

Who should not climb, stated as the Comune states it

The official warnings are firmer than the cheerful tone of most travel writing about this tower, and they deserve repeating without softening.

The climb is strongly advised against for people with heart conditions, respiratory illness, claustrophobia, vertigo or diabetes, for pregnant women, and generally for anyone in poor health. Children under 14 may climb only accompanied by an adult.

There are around 400 steps and no lift. The stairway narrows as it rises, the final sections are enclosed and steep, and there is no way to turn back easily once a group is moving — twenty-five people on a spiral staircase means the person behind you decides your pace as much as you do. Claustrophobia is on that list for a reason.

The tower closes in bad weather, and for restoration and maintenance. A wet or windy morning is not a "we will see when we get there" situation; it is a closed tower.

Torre del Mangia or the Facciatone?

Siena has two great climbs and almost nobody compares them properly, so here it is.

Torre del Mangia — €10, or €15 with the museum

You climb out of the Campo and look down into it. That is the decisive difference: the Torre is the only place you see the shell shape of the Piazza del Campo as a shape, with the paving's nine segments legible below you and the whole city fanning out beyond. It is the view Siena is famous for from the inside.

Against it: 400 steps, no lift, the health restrictions above, no booking, capped slots, weather closures.

The Facciatone — included in the OPA SI Pass

The panorama from the unfinished façade of the "New Cathedral" is included in the OPA SI Pass (€13, or €15 while the marble floor is uncovered), so if you were buying that pass anyway the view costs you nothing extra. It is a shorter climb, and it delivers the one thing the Torre cannot: a view with the Torre del Mangia in it. From up there you also stand on the wall of the cathedral Siena started and never finished after the Black Death — the view and the history are the same object.

Against it: it is a narrow terrace, it can feel exposed, and it does not give you the Campo from directly above.

The honest verdict

If you can only do one and you are fit: the Torre. The Campo from above is the memory people keep.

If you are buying the OPA SI Pass anyway, or the tower's restrictions apply to you, or it is raining: the Facciatone, without regret. It is not a consolation prize — several people who do both prefer it, because a photograph of Siena is better with the tower in it than taken from the tower.

If you have a full day: do both, in that order, and notice that each one contains the other.

What you see from the top

The reason the climb is worth its complications is directly below you, and it is a piece of design rather than a view.

The Campo reads as a diagram from up there. The paving — laid between 1327 and 1349 in knife-shaped red brick — is divided by ten lines of white travertine into nine segments, all converging on the Palazzo Pubblico beneath your feet. The nine are the Governo dei Nove, the merchant oligarchy that ran Siena from the 1280s to the 1350s and commissioned most of what you have come to see; the same nine folds are read as the folds of the Virgin's cloak, Siena's patron and, in the city's own account of itself, its actual sovereign. At ground level it is a handsome slope. From 87 metres it is a government explaining itself in brick.

The cathedral sits at eye level, and that is the point. The tower was raised to match the height of the Duomo's campanile — civic authority and church authority at the same altitude, which in a fourteenth-century city-state was a position rather than a coincidence. Look left of the cathedral and the Facciatone stands there too: the wall of the enormous new cathedral Siena began in the 1330s and abandoned after the plague, with people on top of it looking back at you.

Beyond the roofs, the contrade. Siena's seventeen districts are not neighbourhoods on a map so much as territories, and from above you can follow the ridgelines the city is built along and see how the tiled roofs break into separate quarters down each spur. Our contrade guide explains what you are looking at; the tower is the only place you can see the whole system at once.

And then the countryside starts, immediately. Siena has no suburbs to speak of in the medieval direction — the walls end and the hills begin. On a clear day that abruptness is the most surprising thing about the view, and the best argument for climbing in the morning before the haze sets in.

Hours, seasons and the Palio

Published hours for the Museo Civico, checked 16 August 2026:

  • Summer, 1 March to 31 October: 10:00–13:45 and 14:30–19:00, with the ticket office closing at 18:15.
  • Winter, 1 November to 28 February: 10:00–13:00 and 13:45–16:00, with the ticket office closing at 15:15.

Read the ticket-office time, not the closing time. Arriving at 18:00 in July means the museum is open and the counter is about to shut — and since the tower cannot be bought anywhere else, a closed counter is a closed tower.

Winter shortens the day severely. A 15:15 ticket-office cut-off means a winter visitor who lunches slowly has lost the tower entirely. In November to February, do the climb in the morning.

Palio periods change everything. The Palio runs on 2 July and 16 August, and the Campo is transformed for days around each race — track laid, stands built, the piazza closed to ordinary use. The Comune publishes special Museo Civico and Torre opening hours for those periods. If your dates fall in late June, early July or mid-August, treat the standard schedule above as not applying and check the announcements for your day.

What you are actually climbing

The tower went up between 1338 and 1348 — finished, in other words, in the year the Black Death reached Siena and ended the city's century. It stands about 87 metres, or 102 counting the lightning rod, built in brick with the upper section in travertine, the work of the Sienese sculptor Agostino di Giovanni to a design attributed to Lippo Memmi, on a tower built by the brothers Francesco and Muccio di Rinaldo.

It was built deliberately to match the height of the cathedral's campanile — civic power and church power at the same altitude, which in a fourteenth-century Italian city-state was an argument rather than an aesthetic choice. Standing at the top with the Duomo at eye level is the argument still being made.

The name is a joke that stuck. The first bell-ringer, Giovanni di Balduccio, was nicknamed il mangiaguadagni — the earnings-eater — for spending his wages on food. Seven hundred years later Siena still calls its most famous building after a man who was bad with money.

The great bell at the top, the Campanone or Sunto — dedicated to Mary of the Assumption — was installed in 1666 after several failed castings. It is rung for the Palio, and if you are on the stairs when it sounds you will not forget it.

Fitting it into a day in Siena

The Torre sits in the Piazza del Campo, which means it is three minutes from almost everything and the temptation is to treat it as a drop-in. Do not. It is the one sight in Siena whose availability is decided before 11:00.

A workable order for a full day: ticket office at opening, tower slot, Museo Civico, lunch away from the Campo, cathedral complex in the afternoon on the OPA SI Pass with the Facciatone at the end for the light. Our one day in Siena itinerary lays out the walking, and the day trip versus overnight comparison is worth reading first if you are arriving from Florence — a day-tripper who reaches the ticket office at noon has usually already lost the tower.

How we checked these details

Checked 16 August 2026, by web research against the Comune di Siena's and the Museo Civico's published material; direct page fetches are blocked in our environment, so this rests on search-surfaced official content rather than pages we opened.

Verified: the Torre del Mangia single ticket at €10.00 and the family ticket at €25.00 for two adults plus minors aged 11–18; the Museo Civico at €10.00 (€11.00 with booking) and its €4.50/€5.50 reduced rates; the combined tickets at €15.00 (Museo Civico + Torre, one day), €14.00/€15.00 (Museo Civico + Santa Maria della Scala, two days) and €20.00 (all three); the rule that tickets including the tower are not bookable and are sold only at the Museo Civico and Torre del Mangia ticket office; the condition that on a combined ticket the first entry must be at the tower; ascents every 45 minutes capped at 25 people, with the summer ascent times of 10:00 through 18:00 as listed; approximately 400 steps and no lift; the official warnings against climbing for those with heart, respiratory, claustrophobia, vertigo or diabetes conditions, for pregnant women and for anyone in poor health, and the requirement that under-14s be accompanied; closure in bad weather and for restoration and maintenance; the summer hours of 10:00–13:45 and 14:30–19:00 with the ticket office closing at 18:15, and the winter hours of 10:00–13:00 and 13:45–16:00 with the office closing at 15:15; and the existence of special published Museo Civico and Torre hours around the Palio. The tower's construction between 1338 and 1348, its height of about 87 metres (102 with the lightning rod), its builders Francesco and Muccio di Rinaldo, the travertine upper section by Agostino di Giovanni to a design attributed to Lippo Memmi, the mangiaguadagni nickname of the first bell-ringer Giovanni di Balduccio, and the 1666 installation of the Sunto bell were checked against regional tourism and reference sources, as were the Campo's paving dates of 1327–1349, its division by ten travertine lines into nine segments, and the reading of those nine as both the Governo dei Nove and the folds of the Virgin's cloak.

Flagged as unconfirmed: the winter ascent timetable, which we could not retrieve in the same detail as the summer list; whether the published Museo Civico midday break applies to the tower's own ascent schedule, which shows no gap; the exact Palio-period hours for 2026, which the Comune publishes close to each race; and reduced or free entry categories for the tower specifically. The Facciatone pricing comes from the Opera del Duomo's OPA SI Pass and is documented in our cathedral ticket guide, including the ticketing restructure the Opera made in March 2026.

We have no commercial relationship with the Comune di Siena, the Museo Civico or any ticket seller. No booking made from this page pays us anything, and no reseller is recommended — which matters here more than usual, because the tower cannot legitimately be pre-booked at all.

Final thoughts

Almost everything that goes wrong at the Torre del Mangia goes wrong before anyone reaches the stairs. The ticket cannot be booked, the counter shuts earlier than the museum, the slots are capped at twenty-five, the combined ticket makes you climb first, and rain closes it outright.

None of that is difficult once you know it. Arrive at the ticket office when it opens, take the first slot you are offered, and the rest of the day arranges itself around a climb that is worth arranging a day around. And if the tower says no — wrong weather, wrong health, wrong hour — walk up to the Facciatone instead and photograph the tower from the cathedral it was built to rival.

articles.title: The 17 Contrade of Siena: What They Actually Are
articles.seoTitle: The 17 Contrade of Siena: What They Are, and the 1675 Myth
articles.metaDescription: Siena's 17 contrade explained — the three terzi, the six that died out, why boundaries follow palaces not streets, and how to visit a contrada museum.
articles.excerpt: Siena's contrade are territorial associations with their own legal personality, boundaries fixed by a 1730 edict that named palaces rather than streets, and a membership you are mostly born into. This guide covers the seventeen and their terzi, the six that died out and the 1675 story that did not happen, the seven official rivalries including one that runs only one way, and how contrada museums actually open.

hero.credit: Photo: Razzairpina / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 3.0. Cropped from original.
hero.alt: Colourful Contrada del Bruco flags hanging along a historic street in Siena

faqs.q: How many contrade are there in Siena?
faqs.a: Seventeen, grouped under the three terzi: Città (Aquila, Chiocciola, Onda, Pantera, Selva, Tartuca), San Martino (Civetta, Leocorno, Nicchio, Torre, Valdimontone) and Camollia (Bruco, Drago, Giraffa, Istrice, Lupa, Oca). Six more existed historically — Gallo, Leone, Orso, Quercia, Spadaforte and Vipera — and died out, though all six still appear in the Corteo Storico before each Palio.

faqs.q: Can tourists visit a contrada museum?
faqs.a: Yes, but by prior reservation with the individual contrada. There is no drop-in, no combined or city-wide ticket, and no central booking desk at the Comune or tourist office. Admission is generally free or by voluntary donation, so the reservation rather than the money is the barrier. A few contrade publish limited afternoon hours, and commercial walking tours including a museum visit exist. Arrange it before you travel.

faqs.q: Were the six extinct contrade abolished in 1675?
faqs.a: Almost certainly not, despite the story being repeated confidently. The Sienese documentary record shows Gallo, Leone, Orso, Quercia, Spadaforte and Vipera were already inactive before 1675; they faded through organisational weakness and withdrawal from civic life across the seventeenth century, and their disappearance was formalised only in 1729–30 when the boundary edict recognised seventeen and no more.

faqs.q: Why do contrada boundaries look so irregular?
faqs.a: Because they were defined by naming palaces and their owners rather than streets. The Bando of Violante Beatrice of Bavaria, promulgated 7 January 1730 (1729 in Siena's ab Incarnatione dating, where the year began on 25 March), settled boundaries that had previously been governed by no rule at all and had caused frequent, sometimes violent disputes. It fixed the number at seventeen and remains the working instrument today.

faqs.q: Which contrade are rivals?
faqs.a: Seven pairs are officially recognised on the Palio's own channels — among them Oca and Torre, Istrice and Lupa, and Aquila and Pantera. Torre is the only contrada with two enemies, Oca and Onda. The Onda–Torre rivalry runs one way only: Onda regards Torre as its enemy and Torre does not reciprocate. Four contrade have no official rival at all: Drago, Giraffa, Bruco and Selva.

faqs.q: Do all 17 contrade race in the Palio?
faqs.a: No. Ten run in each Palio, on 2 July and 16 August; the other seven watch from their own territory. Because only ten run, a rivalry can be live with both present, one-sided, or in the Sienese phrase frozen, with both enemies absent. A contrada's year is organised around a race it may not be in.

faqs.q: Can a visitor join or support a contrada?
faqs.a: Not in the way a football club works, and offering to is the move that marks a visitor out. Membership runs through birth in the territory and through family, and where adults do join by affinity it is a commitment confirmed over time. Curiosity is welcome; adopting a contrada as a holiday allegiance is not, because picking is not the mechanism.

articles.bodyHtml:
The contrade are usually introduced as the seventeen teams that race in the Palio. That is roughly as useful as describing a parish as a bingo night.

They are territorial associations with their own legal personality, their own governing offices, their own churches, museums and social clubs, boundaries fixed by an eighteenth-century edict that is still the working instrument today, and a membership you are mostly born into. The race is two afternoons a year. The contrada is the other three hundred and sixty-three days.

Quick answer

There are seventeen contrade, grouped under Siena's three medieval terzi. Ten run in each Palio. Six more contrade existed and died out — and the popular story of how is almost certainly wrong.

The one practical thing to know: every contrada has a museum, and they open by prior arrangement with the individual contrada. There is no drop-in, no combined ticket and no central booking desk. If you want to see inside one, that is a phone call or an email made days ahead, not a decision made on the afternoon.

And the one thing to get right socially: a contrada is not a fan club you can join for a week. Curiosity is welcome; adopting a contrada as a holiday allegiance is the move that marks a visitor out.

The seventeen, and the three terzi

Siena is divided into three terzi — thirds — which are older than the contrade and still organise them.

CittàAquila, Chiocciola, Onda, Pantera, Selva, Tartuca

CamolliaBruco, Drago, Giraffa, Istrice, Lupa, Oca

Each has an emblem and a livery, and the liveries are how you read the streets — the flags, the lamp brackets, the ceramic plaques on building corners.

LupaShe-wolf suckling Romulus and RemusWhite and black with orange
NicchioSeashell with coral branchesBlue with red and yellow
OcaCrowned goose with a Savoy collarWhite and green with red
OndaCrowned dolphinWhite and light blue

SelvaRhinoceros at the foot of an oakGreen and orange with white
TartucaTortoiseYellow and blue
TorreElephant with a tower on its backCrimson with white and blue
ValdimontoneRampant crowned ram on a gold fieldRed and yellow with white

Two details worth having right, because both circulate wrongly. Valdimontone's ram stands on gold, not blue — blue appears only in the small upper-left canton carrying the crowned letter U, added in 1889 by authorisation of Umberto I. And Selva's motto is "Prima Selvalta in campo", from the contrada's older name Selvalta; the widely copied "Prima Selva in campo" is a corruption.

Eight titles, and what they were for

Eight contrade carry an honorific granted for a specific historical service; the other nine carry none.

Nobile: Aquila, Bruco, Nicchio and Oca. Priora: Civetta. Imperiale: Giraffa. Capitana: Onda. Sovrana: Istrice.

Most trace to medieval or early-modern events. Civetta is Priora because it hosted the first meetings of the Comitato dei Priori in 1887, the body that became the Magistrato delle Contrade — the assembly of the seventeen Priors that still coordinates them. Istrice is Sovrana through the Order of Malta, whose Sienese seat and hospital have stood in Istrice territory since the fourteenth century.

And one that deserves a sentence rather than a gloss. Giraffa's Imperiale is not medieval: it comes from winning the Palio of 2 July 1936, which was dedicated to the proclamation of the Italian Empire — the Ethiopian conquest — and run before Vittorio Emanuele III. It is a Fascist-era honorific that the contrada still carries. Guides that translate it as "imperial" and move on are skipping the only interesting thing about it.

The six that died, and the story that did not happen

Siena once had far more contrade. Six are gone: Gallo, Leone, Orso, Quercia, Spadaforte and Vipera.

The story you will be told is that they were abolished by decree after disorder at the Palio of 1675. It is repeated confidently across enthusiast sites and guidebooks, and the documentary support for it is weak. The Sienese record shows these contrade already inactive before 1675: they faded through organisational weakness and withdrawal from civic life across the seventeenth century, and their disappearance was formalised only in 1729–30, when the boundary edict recognised seventeen and no more.

That is a duller story and a truer one, and it says something about how institutions actually end — not by decree, but by nobody turning up.

Their territory was absorbed by their neighbours. The Quercia went into the Chiocciola; the Spadaforte was divided between Leocorno and Torre; the Gallo's and Orso's streets were shared among Civetta, Selva and Oca.

But they are not forgotten, and this is the detail to watch for. All six still appear in the Corteo Storico, the procession before each Palio — each represented by a mounted knight carrying a lance, with a helm bearing the dead contrada's symbol. Siena has been walking its extinct districts through the Campo for three centuries.

Why the boundaries follow palaces, not streets

Contrada territory looks arbitrary on a map because it was not drawn on one.

Before the eighteenth century there was no rule governing where one contrada ended and the next began, and the resulting disputes were frequent and sometimes violent. The fix came from the city's governor, Violante Beatrice of Bavaria, whose Bando sopra la nuova divisione e riforma de' Confini delle Contrade settled the question — promulgated on 7 January 1730 by modern reckoning, and dated 1729 in Sienese usage, because Siena counted the year ab Incarnatione, from 25 March. Both dates are correct; sources using different ones are not contradicting each other.

The edict drew boundaries by naming palaces and their owners rather than by naming streets. That is why a boundary can run through the middle of a block, why one side of a doorway can be in a different contrada from the other, and why the plaques are on building corners rather than at junctions. It fixed the number at seventeen, and it is still the working instrument.

Its purpose was public order rather than sentiment. What it produced, three centuries later, is a city where a five-minute walk crosses three sovereignties.

Rivalries: seven pairs, and one that only runs one way

This is where travel writing romanticises hardest, so here is what is officially recognised rather than what makes a good paragraph.

There are seven official pairs of rival contrade, recognised on the Palio's own official channels — not folklore, not a journalistic invention. Among them: Oca and Torre, Istrice and Lupa, Aquila and Pantera.

Torre is the only contrada with two enemies — Oca and Onda.

And the Onda–Torre rivalry runs in one direction only: Onda regards Torre as its enemy, and Torre does not reciprocate the recognition. Being someone's rival without their agreement is, if you think about it, worse than mutual hatred.

Four contrade have no official rival at all: Drago, Giraffa, Bruco and Selva.

Because only ten of seventeen run each race, a rivalry can be live (both present), one-sided (one racing, one watching) or, in the Sienese phrase, frozen — both enemies absent, nothing to settle. It is entirely possible for a contrada to regard stopping its rival as the better outcome than winning, and that logic shapes the race in ways an outsider watching for speed will not see.

How the contrade meet the Palio

Ten of the seventeen run in each Palio, on 2 July and 16 August. The rest watch — from their own territory, which is a different experience from watching as a visitor.

The mechanics of who runs, how horses are assigned, and what the four days actually contain are a separate subject, and we cover them in our Palio di Siena guide — including the honest case for choosing a different week.

What belongs here is the consequence: a contrada's year is organised around a race it may not be in. That is the part that makes no sense from outside and complete sense from inside.

Visiting a contrada museum — how it actually works

This is the section we most want you to read, because the common advice is wrong in a way that wastes an afternoon.

Every one of the seventeen contrade has its own museum, generally alongside its oratory and its società. They hold the drappelloni the contrada has won, the masgalani, old and new monture — the procession costumes — antique banners, sacred furnishings and works of art. The finest room is always the Sala delle Vittorie, which frequently doubles as the hall where the contrada's General Council meets.

They open by prior reservation with the individual contrada. That is the official position, and the practical consequences follow from it:

  • There is no drop-in. Turning up at a contrada's door on the day will usually find it locked.
  • There is no combined or city-wide ticket. Each contrada manages its own museum independently.
  • There is no central booking desk at the Comune or the tourist office that will arrange it for you. You contact the contrada.
  • Admission is generally free or by voluntary donation rather than a fixed charge — which makes the reservation, not the money, the barrier.
  • A few contrade publish limited opening hours — the Leocorno's museum is one — but these are the exception and are commonly afternoon-only, with mornings and Sundays still by appointment.
  • Commercial walking tours that include a contrada museum exist, and for a visitor with two days and no Italian they are the pragmatic route in. Guided visits arranged directly with a contrada are often in Italian, with English by request.

So the honest advice is: decide before you travel. If a contrada museum matters to you, write to one a week ahead, or book a tour that includes one. If you only realise you want it on the second morning, take the flags and the streets instead — which cost nothing and are always open.

Walking the territories

You do not need a museum to see the system working. The observable layer is free and continuous.

Look for the plaques on building corners carrying a contrada's arms — that is the boundary, and it is why the marker is on a wall rather than at a crossroads. Look up for the lamp brackets and flag holders in contrada colours. And find the fountains: each contrada has its own fontanina, the baptismal fountain where new members are received into the contrada in a lay ceremony of its own.

From the Campo, walking uphill toward the cathedral and back down the far side will cross several territories inside an hour, and the change of colours as you pass a corner is the whole point made without a word. Our Siena walking tour covers the route; the one-day itinerary fits it around the ticketed sights.

How to be a good visitor

Two facts established above do most of the work here, and they are better guidance than any list of tips.

First, a contrada is a legal person, not a theme. It owns property, elects officers, holds assemblies and buries its members. Its museum is private property opened by invitation; its società is a members' club. Approaching any of it as a public amenity is the error, and it is a category error rather than a rudeness.

Second, membership is not chosen the way a football club is. It runs through birth in the territory and through family, and where adults do join by affinity it is a commitment confirmed over time. That is why announcing that you have "picked" a contrada for the week lands badly: it is not that you have picked the wrong one, it is that picking is not the mechanism.

Beyond that, the ordinary courtesies apply and are enough: ask before photographing people, do not walk through a procession, and treat a rivalry as something to be curious about rather than to joke about with someone who lives inside it.

What we could not establish

An unusual section, but this subject is unusually badly served by confident writing, and we would rather show you the edge of what we checked.

  • Membership numbers. There is no current census of contradaioli. The last city-wide figures date from 1954, and contrada officials have said publicly that a comprehensive count would be very hard to conduct. Any total you see quoted should be treated as an estimate.
  • The full list of seven rival pairs. We verified that seven officially recognised pairs exist and confirmed several of them; we did not enumerate all seven from a primary source in this session.
  • Each contrada's patron saint and titular feast date. These govern when a contrada baptises and celebrates, and we could not assemble a reliable list.
  • The contrada baptism in detail — who officiates, how often it is held, and the claim that the Chiocciola revived the rite in 1949 and the practice then spread. Widely repeated; not confirmed here.
  • Horse welfare and the veterinary regime. This is the question most English-speaking readers arrive with, and we have not researched it to a standard we would publish. We would rather say so than fill the space with sentiment. It belongs in our Palio coverage and is on our list.

How we checked these details

Checked 16 August 2026, by web research; direct page fetches are blocked in our environment, so this rests on search-surfaced material rather than pages we opened.

Verified against the Comune di Siena and the official Palio channels: the seventeen contrade and their names; their distribution across the three terzi; the emblems and colours listed above, including the Comune's own description of Valdimontone's arms as a rampant crowned ram on a gold field with the crowned letter U on blue in the upper-left canton, authorised in 1889; the eight honorific titles and which contrade hold them; Civetta's Priora title deriving from its hosting of the first Comitato dei Priori in 1887, the body that became the Magistrato delle Contrade; Istrice's Sovrana title through the Order of Malta's Sienese seat since the fourteenth century; Giraffa's Imperiale title deriving from the Palio of 2 July 1936 dedicated to the proclamation of the Italian Empire; the six extinct contrade, the absorption of their territories, and their continuing representation in the Corteo Storico by mounted knights; the Bando of Violante Beatrice of Bavaria promulgated 7 January 1730 modern style and 1729 Sienese style under the ab Incarnatione calendar, its fixing of the number at seventeen and its definition of boundaries by named palaces and owners; the existence of seven officially recognised rival pairs, Torre as the only contrada with two enemies, the unilateral character of the Onda–Torre rivalry, and Drago, Giraffa, Bruco and Selva having no official rival; that ten of seventeen run each Palio; and that every contrada has a museum, that the museums open by prior reservation with the individual contrade, and that their principal room is the Sala delle Vittorie holding drappelloni, masgalani, monture, banners, sacred furnishings and artworks.

Corrected during checking: Selva's motto, which the contrada and the official Palio site give as "Prima Selvalta in campo" rather than the widely copied "Prima Selva in campo"; Valdimontone's shield, commonly described as blue when the field is gold; and the 1675 dissolution story for the six extinct contrade, which the Sienese documentary record does not support — those contrade were already inactive before that date.

Sourced to visitor-information and commercial channels rather than official ones, and flagged as such: that admission to contrada museums is generally free or by donation; that a small number of contrade publish limited afternoon opening hours; and that commercial walking tours including a contrada museum are available. Confirm access arrangements with the contrada itself before travelling.

We have no commercial relationship with any contrada, with the Comune di Siena, or with any tour operator. No booking made from this page pays us anything, and no tour is recommended.

Final thoughts

The contrade are the reason Siena feels different from every other beautiful Tuscan hill town, and the reason is not pageantry. It is that a medieval territorial settlement — palaces named in a 1730 edict — is still the live organising fact of people's social lives, their marriages, their funerals and their arguments.

You will not get inside that in three days, and the attempt is what goes wrong. What you can do is learn to read the corners, notice when the colours change, understand that the four contrade with no enemy are not the friendly ones but the unallocated ones, and accept that the most interesting thing in the city is not open to you. Siena is unusually good at being looked at without being consumed. Let it.

articles.bodyHtml:
Finding a good meal in Siena is less about chasing one famous address and more about choosing the right area, reading the menu and matching the stop to your itinerary.

This guide focuses on durable advice rather than a list of restaurants that may change hours, ownership or quality. It shows where to look and which Sienese dishes deserve attention.

Quick answer

For convenience, eat near Via di Città or Via Banchi di Sopra. For a quieter atmosphere, explore streets toward Piazza del Mercato. Choose a terrace on Piazza del Campo mainly for the view. Look for pici, pecorino, Cinta Senese products, ribollita, ricciarelli and panforte.

Piazza del Campo: best for the setting

The Campo is the easiest place to pause and the hardest place to judge value. A prominent terrace gives you one of Siena’s best dining views, but location is built into the price.

Use the Campo for coffee, an aperitivo or a meal when the setting is the priority. Compare the menu, cover charge and recent reviews before sitting down.

Via di Città and the streets between the Campo and Duomo

This central corridor works well for travellers following a one-day itinerary. It offers cafés, bakeries, wine bars and restaurants without requiring a major detour.

The busiest frontage can still feel tourist-oriented, so inspect side streets and menus rather than choosing the first host who approaches you.

Via Banchi di Sopra

Via Banchi di Sopra is useful for a quick breakfast, pastry, coffee or casual lunch. Its central position makes it practical before or after Piazza del Campo.

Look for places with clear pricing and a menu sized to the kitchen. An enormous menu covering every Italian region is rarely the strongest signal for a focused Sienese meal.

Piazza del Mercato and nearby streets

The area behind Palazzo Pubblico can feel calmer than the Campo while remaining close to the centre. It suits travellers who want a lunch break away from the busiest view corridor.

Combine the meal with a short walk toward Orto de’ Pecci or the southern lanes of the historic centre.

What to eat in Siena

Visit Tuscany identifies pici as a thick hand-rolled pasta typical of Siena. Sauces vary, including aglione and meat-based preparations. Pecorino and Cinta Senese products are also closely associated with the area.

For sweets, try ricciarelli, panforte, cavallucci or panpepato. Panforte is available beyond the Christmas season, while ricciarelli pair naturally with coffee or Vin Santo.

How to choose a restaurant

Check the current menu, recent photographs and reviews from the last few months. Look for a realistic number of dishes, seasonal ingredients and transparent pricing.

Confirm opening days on the restaurant’s own channel and call or message for important reservations. Map listings are useful but not infallible.

Lunch timing and reservations

Plan lunch around your cathedral visit rather than risking a timed attraction. During weekends, holidays and floor-uncovering periods, reserve a place you strongly prefer.

A flexible backup is more useful than a rigid list. Save two or three options in the same area so a closure does not disrupt the day.

Dietary needs

Ask directly about ingredients and cross-contamination. Pici recipes, soups, sauces and desserts vary, and a familiar dish name does not guarantee identical preparation.

Learn a short Italian phrase for your allergy and carry written details when the risk is serious.

Frequently asked questions

What food is Siena known for?

Pici, pecorino, Cinta Senese products, ricciarelli and panforte are strong starting points.

Is it expensive to eat on Piazza del Campo?

The location often carries a premium. Read the menu and charges before ordering.

Do I need reservations?

They are useful for a specific restaurant, weekends and busy travel periods, but casual alternatives are widely available.

Final thoughts

The best Siena meal fits the pace of your day and gives you a sense of place. Choose the area deliberately, read the menu and leave enough time to enjoy the food instead of eating between alarms.

articles.bodyHtml:
Siena is best understood on foot. The lanes climb, narrow and open without warning, turning a short route into a sequence of civic spaces, contrada symbols and rooftop views.

This self-guided Siena walking tour covers the essential historic centre in roughly half a day, excluding long museum visits. Walking times are estimates and the route includes hills, cobbles and steps.

Quick answer

Start at Piazza del Campo, walk to the Duomo, continue through Via di Città, explore the streets toward Piazza del Mercato and Orto de’ Pecci, then loop back to the Campo. Allow three to four hours with stops, or a full day when adding the cathedral and lunch.

Before you start

Wear comfortable shoes and download an offline map. The route is compact but not flat. Travellers with mobility needs should review each segment and use alternative approaches where steps appear.

Begin early for quieter streets or in mid-afternoon if you want to finish around aperitivo time.

Stop 1: Piazza del Campo

Begin on the upper curve and walk down toward Palazzo Pubblico. Notice the shell shape, paving divisions and the way the surrounding façades form a continuous civic room.

Allow 20–30 minutes without a museum, longer if you add the Museo Civico or tower.

Stop 2: Palazzo Pubblico and Torre del Mangia

Stand near the base of the tower and look back across the square. Decide here whether to purchase a same-day tower ticket. Do not build the entire walk around the climb unless you have confirmed a slot.

Stop 3: Via di Città

Leave the Campo toward Via di Città. This historic route carries you toward the cathedral through a mix of shops, palazzi and side lanes.

Pause at openings that reveal the layered roofs rather than walking only with the next landmark in view.

Stop 4: Piazza del Duomo

The cathedral façade is the visual climax of the uphill section. Walk around the square before entering so you understand the relationship between the Duomo, Santa Maria della Scala and the slope of the site.

A cathedral visit changes this from a walking tour into a half-day itinerary. Allow at least 60–90 minutes inside.

Stop 5: Santa Maria della Scala

Cross the piazza to the former hospital complex. If you are not entering, note how the two institutions face each other. If you visit, allow at least 90 minutes and resume the walk afterward.

Stop 6: Contrada streets

Move away from the direct Campo–Duomo corridor and look for flags, emblems and fountains. The official municipal site recognizes 17 contrade, each with a distinct identity.

Stay on public streets and avoid entering community spaces without an invitation or clear visitor access.

Stop 7: Piazza del Mercato

Descend toward the space behind Palazzo Pubblico for a different view of Siena’s civic centre. This area can feel calmer than the Campo and works well for a food break.

Stop 8: Orto de’ Pecci and return

If time and weather allow, continue toward Orto de’ Pecci for a greener perspective below the centre, then climb back toward Piazza del Campo. The return is uphill, so leave enough energy and daylight.

Self-guided or guided?

A self-guided route offers flexibility and costs nothing. A good local guide adds context about the contrade, Palio, civic art and political history that is difficult to reconstruct from façades alone.

Choose a tour based on content, group size and route—not only price. Confirm whether cathedral entry is included or separate.

Frequently asked questions

How long is a Siena walking tour?

Allow three to four hours for this outdoor route with pauses, or a full day with the cathedral, museums and lunch.

Is the route difficult?

It is moderate because Siena is hilly and cobbled. Adjust it for mobility, heat and weather.

Do walking tours include cathedral tickets?

Inclusions vary. Read the exact product description and compare it with official Opera Duomo admission.

Final thoughts

The route is a framework, not a race. Follow the major landmarks, then allow Siena’s side streets to interrupt the plan. Those small deviations are often the best part of the walk.
